blocks.text: 1. Context Window

blocks.alt: Input tokens fill a context window up to a maximum token limit

blocks.text: Context Window covers how much text a model can actually condition on at once, a real, practical limit on every generation call.
It is the hard limit on how far back a model can look before predicting the next token.
2. Recapping The Preview
Next Token Prediction introduced context window briefly, as the limit on how far back a model can look when predicting each token.
Here, that limit gets full treatment: what sets it, why it exists, and what happens when text exceeds it.
3. A Fixed Maximum Token Count

blocks.alt: A model has a fixed maximum token count

blocks.text: Every model architecture defines one fixed maximum number of tokens it can process at once, building on the token IDs introduced in Tokenization.
Anything beyond that maximum simply cannot fit into a single forward pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Context window size","Approximate capacity"],"rows":[["A few thousand tokens","Roughly a few pages of text"],["Hundreds of thousands of tokens","Roughly an entire book"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Why Attention Scales Quadratically

blocks.alt: A sequence length n causes cost to grow as n squared

blocks.text: Self-attention compares every token against every other token, as covered in Attention Mechanism, so doubling the context window quadruples the number of pairwise comparisons attention must compute.
This quadratic cost is the core reason context windows cannot simply grow without limit.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This quadratic scaling directly explains why simply increasing the context window is not a free architectural change, even though longer context is often desirable.

blocks.text: 5. Recapping Positional Embeddings
A model's positional scheme, covered in Positional Embeddings, has to support at least as many positions as its context window.
Exceeding that maximum position breaks the model's ability to represent order correctly.
6. Truncation And Sliding Windows

blocks.alt: A long document is handled by a sliding window or truncation

blocks.text: Text longer than the context window has to be truncated or split into smaller chunks.
This loses everything outside the current window, unless a sliding window strategy is used instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Behavior"],"rows":[["Truncation","Drops text outside the fixed context window entirely"],["Sliding window","Processes overlapping chunks, retaining more of the original text"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Context Window Versus Memory

blocks.alt: A context window is temporary while memory is persistent

blocks.text: A model has no memory of anything outside its own current context window.
Every single generation call starts fresh from whatever text is currently inside that window, an important, often misunderstood distinction.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This distinction explains why applications needing longer-term memory typically rely on external retrieval systems rather than the model's own context window alone.

blocks.text: 8. Growing Context Windows Over Time

blocks.alt: Context windows grew from 4K tokens to 32K to over 128K

blocks.text: Newer architectural techniques have pushed real context windows from a few thousand tokens toward hundreds of thousands.
This happens without fully escaping the quadratic cost of attention, and remains an ongoing area of active improvement.
9. Recognizing Why Context Window Size Is A Real Practical Constraint

blocks.alt: A task needing long input requires checking the context window size

blocks.text: Longer documents need to fit within that fixed limit.
The prompt is the actual text placed inside that window; Prompting, the next topic in this module, explores exactly how that text gets structured.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates truncating text to fit a fixed context window, using a simple token count limit.

code.content:
def tokenize(text):
    # word level splitting
    return text.split()

def fit_to_context_window(tokens, max_tokens):
    # keep only the most recent tokens that fit
    if len(tokens) <= max_tokens:
        return tokens, False
    return tokens[-max_tokens:], True

long_document = ("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog " * 3).split()
context_window_size = 12  # the fixed maximum token count for this example

fitted_tokens, was_truncated = fit_to_context_window(long_document, context_window_size)

print(f"Original document length: {len(long_document)} tokens")
print(f"Context window size: {context_window_size} tokens")
print(f"Was truncated: {was_truncated}")
print(f"\nTokens that actually fit in the context window: {fitted_tokens}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows a document longer than the context window getting cut down to only its most recent tokens, losing everything earlier in the document.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Context window is the hard limit on how far back a model can look before predicting the next token.
Every model architecture defines one fixed maximum number of tokens it can process at once.
Doubling the context window quadruples attention's pairwise comparison cost, limiting how large it can grow.
A model's positional scheme must support at least as many positions as its context window.
Text longer than the window must be truncated or split, unless a sliding window strategy is used.
A model has no memory of anything outside its current context window; every call starts fresh.
Newer techniques have pushed real context windows much larger, without fully escaping the quadratic cost.
Longer documents must fit within this fixed limit, a real practical constraint.
